description: Fig. 3 is a five-panel composite figure reporting the mechanical behaviour of Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C low-density steels with x = 4, 6, 8 and 10 wt% Al (curves labelled 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, 10Al; colour code in (a), (c) and (d): 4Al black, 6Al red, 8Al blue, 10Al green). (a) Engineering stress-strain curves, y = Engineering stress (MPa) 0-1000, x = Engineering strain 0.0-0.6. (b) Mechanical-property summary versus Al content (wt%), left y = Strength (MPa) 200-1000, right y = Elongation (%) 0-80; legend entries YS and UTS (dark squares) and UEL and TEL (red symbols). (c) True stress-true strain curves, y = True stress (Mpa) 0-1400, x = True strain 0.0-0.4. (d) Strain hardening rate (Mpa) 0-4000 versus True strain, with colour-coded stage labels A-E and dashed vertical stage boundaries. (e) Microhardness (HV) 150-350 versus True strain 0.00-0.25 for 4Al (black squares), 8Alγ (red circles) and 8Alα (blue triangles), with a small downward arrow marking the initial ferrite softening. The panels together argue that the 8Al ferrite-based duplex steel delivers the best strength-ductility balance through multi-stage strain hardening of ferrite, whereas 10Al is brittle.

observations.observation: Panel (a) plots engineering stress (MPa, 0-1000) against engineering strain (0.0-0.6) with the legend 4Al (black), 6Al (red), 8Al (blue) and 10Al (green).

The 10Al green curve in (a) rises steeply to a high engineering stress and terminates at a very small engineering strain (before the 0.05 gridline), i.e. brittle behaviour with almost no uniform elongation.
In (a) the 4Al and 6Al curves run closely together and extend beyond engineering strain 0.4, whereas the 8Al curve lies clearly above them before dropping at a smaller strain.
Panel (b) uses a double y-axis (Strength (MPa) 200-1000 left; Elongation (%) 0-80 right) against Al content (wt%) from 4 to 10, with legend entries YS, UTS, UEL and TEL.
In (b) the YS curve (dark filled squares) is the lowest and rises monotonically with Al content, while the UTS curve (dark open squares) is highest at 4 wt% Al and decreases towards 10 wt% Al.
In (b) both elongation curves (red symbols) decrease with increasing Al content, with the sharpest drop occurring between 8 and 10 wt% Al.

Panel (c) plots true stress (Mpa, 0-1400) against true strain (0.0-0.4); the 8Al curve lies highest, peaking between the 800 and 1000 MPa gridlines at a true strain near 0.3, while 4Al and 6Al peak between the 600 and 800 MPa gridlines at larger true strain.

Panel (d) plots strain hardening rate (Mpa, 0-4000) against true strain and is annotated with the stage letters A, B, C, D and E placed next to colour-matched curves, with short dashed vertical lines marking stage boundaries.
In (d) the 10Al curve (green) drops to zero hardening within the first ~0.05 true strain, i.e. much earlier than the other three steels.

Panel (e) plots microhardness (HV, 150-350) against true strain (0.00-0.25) for three series with error bars: 4Al (black squares), 8Alγ (red circles) and 8Alα (blue triangles); all three increase with strain and 8Alα is the highest at every strain.
In (e) a downward arrow marks a small initial decrease of the 8Alα (ferrite) microhardness at the lowest true strains before it rises again.

The caption states that (a) shows engineering stress-strain curves, (b) mechanical properties, (c) true stress-strain curves, (d) strain hardening rate-strain curves and (e) microhardness for 4Al, 6Al, 8Al and 10Al steels.
The citing text states that as Al increases from 4 wt% to 8 wt%, yield strength and tensile strength increase while uniform elongation decreases only from 38 % to 31 %.

The citing text states that at 10 % Al the yield strength increases to 585 MPa but the tensile elongation is only about 4.6 %, exhibiting brittle characteristics attributed to coarsening of DO3 ordered domains and formation of 18R martensite.

The citing text states that 4Al and 6Al steels exhibit three-stage strain hardening labelled A, D and E, whereas 8Al displays five stages A, B, C, D and E, which is unlike conventional ferrite-based duplex steels.

The citing text states that microhardness of austenite in both 4Al and 8Al steels increases with strain, whereas the ferrite of 8Al steel initially decreases and then increases, indicating ferrite softening in the early stages of deformation.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves (Engineering stress (MPa) 0-1000 vs Engineering strain 0.0-0.6) for 4Al (black), 6Al (red), 8Al (blue) and 10Al (green). 8Al reaches the highest curve, 4Al and 6Al reach lower plateaus but extend to the largest strains, and 10Al rises steeply to a high stress yet terminates at very small strain (before 0.05).

Line plot of Strength (MPa, left axis 200-1000) and Elongation (%, right axis 0-80) against Al content (wt%, 4-10), with legend YS, UTS, UEL and TEL. Yield strength and tensile strength rise with Al content up to 8 wt%, while uniform and total elongation fall, with the steepest drop at 10 wt%.

True stress-true strain curves (True stress (Mpa) 0-1400 vs True strain 0.0-0.4) for the same four steels. 8Al attains the highest true stress, peaking between the 800 and 1000 MPa gridlines near true strain 0.3; 4Al and 6Al peak lower but at larger true strain, and 10Al reaches only a short low-strain segment.

Strain hardening rate (Mpa, 0-4000) versus True strain for all four steels, annotated with colour-coded stage letters A-E and dashed vertical lines marking stage boundaries; the 10Al green curve falls to zero within a very small strain, while the 8Al blue curve shows the largest number of labelled stages.

Microhardness (HV, 150-350) versus True strain (0.00-0.25) for 4Al (black squares), 8Alγ (red circles) and 8Alα (blue triangles), each with error bars. All three rise with strain; 8Alα is the highest, and a small downward arrow marks a shallow decrease in 8Alα at the smallest strains.

unreadable_items: panel (b): individual strength/elongation values are not printed as data labels; only axis ticks are available, so values can only be located relative to gridlines
panels (a), (c), (d): no numeric values are printed on the curves, so peak stresses and stage-boundary strains can only be read against gridlines
panel (d): the small colour-coded stage letters (A-E) and their dashed stage-boundary markers are only marginally legible at the supplied resolution
panel (e): the meaning of the small downward arrow is explained only by the citing text, not by an in-panel label
